41188: Isaiah has been called 'the fifth gospel'. The New Testament quotes it more than any prophet. John the Baptist is the voice crying in the wilderness (Isa 40:3; Mark 1:2-3); Jesus announces the year of the Lord's favour from Isa 61 (Luke 4:18-21) and says the Son of Man came to serve and give his life a ransom for many, language widely heard as echoing Isa 53 (Mark 10:45). Philip explains Isa 53:7-8 to the Ethiopian official as being about Jesus (Acts 8:32-35), and Peter applies 'by his wounds you have been healed' to the cross (1 Pet 2:24). Jewish interpreters read the Servant mainly as Israel or a righteous remnant and the royal oracles of a future human Messiah; they also question whether Isa 7:14 refers to a virgin conception, since the Hebrew *almah* means 'young woman'. Christians respond that the Servant both represents Israel and does for Israel what Israel could not, and that Matthew's use of Isa 7:14 follows the Greek *parthenos*.
41189: Isa 53:5 as a guarantee of physical healing now
41190: 'By his stripes we are healed' means healing of bodily sickness is included in the atonement exactly as forgiveness is, so believers can claim healing now by faith.
41191: In Isa 53 the Servant's wounds deal mainly with sin and its consequences: 'he was pierced for our transgressions'. 'Healing' is a frequent prophetic picture for restoring a sinful people (Isa 1:5-6; Isa 6:10). Matthew does apply Isa 53:4 to Jesus' healing ministry (Matt 8:16-17), while Peter applies verse 5 to forgiveness (1 Pet 2:24). Scholars such as Craig Keener and John Oswalt note both dimensions.
41192: Pentecostal and charismatic scholars (e.g. Keener, Gordon Fee in a qualified way) agree healing flows from Christ's work and is a foretaste of the kingdom, while warning against claiming it as an automatic right. Reformed scholars such as Thomas Schreiner say physical healing is guaranteed in the resurrection, not necessarily now. Most agree the 'guarantee now' form is a popular overreach.
41193: A guarantee reading leaves sick believers blamed for weak faith; a fuller reading holds out real hope of healing while trusting God through suffering.
41194: Isaiah 7:14 as only a far-future prediction
41195: Isaiah 7:14 is a straightforward prediction about Jesus' virgin birth with no meaning for King Ahaz in 734 BC.
41196: The sign was given to Ahaz: before the child knows right from wrong, the two kings he feared would be gone (Isa 7:16), which happened within a few years. Many scholars think a child born in Isaiah's day fulfilled the sign first, while Isa 9:6-7 and Isa 11 widen it to a royal child whose names exceed any ordinary king. Matthew then reads the whole pattern as fulfilled in Jesus. Scholars such as John Walton and Craig Blomberg defend this 'double' or typological fulfilment.
41197: Some conservative scholars (e.g. Alec Motyer, Edward J. Young) argue Isa 7:14 is directly and only messianic, noting the unusual wording, the Greek *parthenos*, and the link with Isa 9:6. This is a genuine scholarly disagreement, not just a popular error.
41198: Seeing the original setting shows that God's promises speak into real crises, and that New Testament 'fulfilment' often means filling full a pattern, not only matching a prediction.
41199: Isaiah called Judah to trust God rather than empires, warned that holiness requires justice, and gave exiles reasons to believe God had not abandoned them and would bring them home.
41200: Isaiah still calls God's people to justice for the vulnerable and honest worship, offers comfort to those who feel forgotten, and holds out the hope of a renewed creation where swords become ploughshares and every nation worships.
41201: A reluctant priest-prophet spends forty years telling Jerusalem that its covenant-breaking will bring Babylon, suffers rejection for it, and then promises a homecoming and a new covenant written on the heart.
41202: Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, with his scribe Baruch
41203: A young man from a priestly family in Anathoth, a village about 5 km north-east of Jerusalem, possibly descended from Abiathar, the priest Solomon banished there (1 Kgs 2:26). Called as a youth in 627 BC, he was forbidden to marry (Jer 16:1-4), was beaten, put in stocks, imprisoned and thrown into a muddy cistern, and was finally taken to Egypt against his will.
41204: The book tells us Jeremiah dictated his oracles to Baruch son of Neriah, that King Jehoiakim burned the scroll column by column, and that Jeremiah dictated it again 'with many similar words added' (Jer 36:4; Jer 36:23; Jer 36:32). This is the Bible's clearest description of how a prophetic book was written. The Greek Septuagint version is about one-eighth shorter and arranged differently, and Hebrew fragments from Qumran support both forms, so the book clearly grew in stages.
41206: 1-2 Kings (credited to him by the Talmud, Bava Batra 15a)
41208: Most oracles were delivered in Jerusalem, many in the temple courts. Jeremiah's last recorded words were spoken at Tahpanhes in the eastern Nile Delta (Jer 43:8-13; Jer 44:1).
41209: Kings, priests, prophets and people of Judah, then the exiles in Babylon and refugees in Egypt
41211: Judah was caught between Egypt and Babylon. Many believed that because the temple stood in Jerusalem, God would never let the city fall. Jeremiah's message that Babylon was God's instrument sounded like treason.
41212: From Jeremiah's call in Josiah's 13th year to the release of King Jehoiachin from prison in Babylon, the book's final scene (Jer 52:31-34).
41213: The book of the law is found in the temple and Josiah's reform begins (2 Kgs 22-23).
41214: Nineveh falls to the Babylonians and Medes; Assyria collapses.
41215: Nebuchadnezzar defeats Egypt at Carchemish (Jer 46:2), making Babylon master of the Levant.
41216: Babylon captures Jerusalem and deports King Jehoiachin, recorded in the Babylonian Chronicle.
41217: Lachish letters: an officer writes that he can no longer see Azekah's signals, matching Jer 34:7 (dating approximate).
41218: Jerusalem and the temple are destroyed; Gedaliah is appointed governor and later murdered (Jer 39-41).
41219:
Jeremiah's forty-year ministry spans the end of the kingdom of Judah. It began under Josiah, the reforming king who purged idols after the 'book of the law' was found (622 BC). Josiah's death at Megiddo in 609 BC, fighting Pharaoh Necho, shattered hopes. His sons Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim and Zedekiah, and his grandson Jehoiachin, swung between Egypt and Babylon. Jehoiakim burned Jeremiah's scroll in his winter palace; Zedekiah consulted Jeremiah secretly but lacked the courage to obey.

Jeremiah's most dangerous message was the temple sermon (Jer 7; Jer 26). Standing at the temple gate, he told worshippers not to trust the slogan 'the temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD' while they stole, murdered, committed adultery and followed other gods. He warned that the temple could become like Shiloh, the earlier sanctuary destroyed long before. He was nearly executed; elders saved him by recalling that the prophet Micah had said something similar a century earlier and had not been killed (Jer 26:16-19).

Jeremiah's confrontation with false prophets is equally sharp. Hananiah prophesied that Babylon's yoke would be broken within two years and broke the wooden yoke Jeremiah was wearing as a sign; Jeremiah replied that God would replace it with iron (Jer 28). Jeremiah urged surrender to Babylon as God's will for the time, which made him look like a traitor.

Archaeology has given the book unusual texture. Clay seal impressions (bullae) bearing the names of Gemariah son of Shaphan (Jer 36:10), Jehucal son of Shelemiah and Gedaliah son of Pashhur (Jer 38:1) have been found in Jerusalem, and the Lachish letters (about 588 BC) show the panic of the Babylonian advance. A bulla reading 'Berekhyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe', once linked to Baruch, is now widely suspected to be a forgery.
41221: Prophets acted out their messages: Jeremiah buried a linen loincloth until it rotted, smashed a clay jar before the elders, wore an ox yoke, and bought a field while Jerusalem was under siege to show that land would one day be bought again.
41223: Jeremiah speaks like a prosecutor bringing God's case against a faithless wife or son, calling heaven and earth as witnesses, in the style of Deuteronomy.
41225: Jeremiah's private complaints to God, unique among the prophets, accuse God of deceiving him and curse the day of his birth, yet he cannot stop speaking: the word is like fire in his bones.
41227: Jeremiah watches a potter reshape a spoiled pot and learns that God may change announced plans if a nation repents, or a promised blessing if it turns to evil.
41228: A round number for a lifetime of exile, from Babylon's rise (about 605 BC) to its fall (539 BC). Daniel later prays over this prophecy and Chronicles sees it fulfilled in Cyrus.
41230: Under the Torah a kinsman could buy back family land to keep it in the clan. Jeremiah's purchase of his cousin's field at Anathoth used sealed deeds stored in a clay jar, the same method that preserved the Dead Sea Scrolls.
41231:
Jeremiah shapes the Jewish calendar of mourning. In the three weeks between the fast of 17 Tammuz and Tisha B'Av, two of the three special 'haftarot of affliction' are read from Jeremiah (Jer 1 and Jer 2), and on the morning of Tisha B'Av the prophetic reading is Jer 8:13-9:23, with its cry 'Oh that my head were waters and my eyes a fountain of tears' (Jer 9:1). Tradition calls him 'the weeping prophet' and credits him with Lamentations. On the second day of Rosh Hashanah the haftarah is from Jer 31, where Rachel weeps for her children and God answers, 'Is Ephraim my dear son? ... I will surely have mercy on him'. Many Jews still visit the traditional Tomb of Rachel near Bethlehem in connection with this text.

Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (Jer 29) became a charter for Jewish life in the diaspora: build houses, plant gardens, marry, and 'seek the welfare (*shalom*) of the city' where God has sent you, praying for it (Jer 29:5-7). Jewish communities have long prayed for the governments of the lands where they live, a practice rooted partly in this passage.

Read covenantally, Jeremiah is a love story gone wrong and then renewed. God remembers Israel's 'devotion' as a young bride following him in the wilderness (Jer 2:2), accuses her of running after other lovers, and grieves like a wounded husband and father (Jer 3:19-20; Jer 31:20). The judgment is the covenant curse of Deuteronomy, but it is not God's last word. The new covenant of Jer 31:31-34 is made 'with the house of Israel and the house of Judah'; its newness lies not in a new Torah but in Torah written on the heart, so that all will know the LORD and sin will be forgiven.
41233: God appoints a reluctant youth as prophet to the nations, to uproot and to plant.
41235: God indicts Israel for leaving the fountain of living water for broken cisterns and calls her to return.
41237: The temple sermon: God's house is not a lucky charm for people who break his covenant.
41239: Sign-acts, rejection and laments: Jeremiah suffers with and for his people.
41241: Jeremiah confronts kings and false prophets, wears a yoke, and tells exiles to settle for seventy years.
41243: God promises restoration, Rachel's comfort and a new covenant written on hearts; Jeremiah buys a field in hope.
41245: Jeremiah is imprisoned and rescued from a cistern; Jerusalem falls and survivors flee to Egypt, dragging him along.
41247: Oracles against Egypt, Philistia, Moab, Babylon and others; the book ends with Jehoiachin freed in Babylon, a flicker of hope.
41267: To turn back, return; used over 100 times in Jeremiah, both for Israel turning back to God and God turning back their captivity.
41268: A binding relationship sealed by oath, with commitments on both sides; here broken by Israel and renewed by God.
41270: To know by experience and relationship, not just facts. In the new covenant all will know the LORD.
41272: Wholeness, wellbeing, prosperity. False prophets cry 'peace' when there is none; exiles are to seek Babylon's shalom.
41274: Plans, intentions. In Jer 29:11 God's plans are for the exiled community's future after seventy years.
41275: Jeremiah's language of covenant, curse and circumcised hearts draws heavily on Deuteronomy, likely the book found in Josiah's reign.
41276: Kings narrates the same final kings and the fall of Jerusalem; Jer 52 closely parallels 2 Kgs 24-25.
41277: Lamentations mourns the fall Jeremiah predicted and is traditionally credited to him.
41278: Daniel prays over Jeremiah's seventy years and receives a vision of seventy 'weeks' of years.
41279: Hebrews quotes Jer 31:31-34 at length, the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament.
41280: Matthew applies Rachel weeping for her children to Herod's massacre in Bethlehem, and Jesus combines Jer 7:11 with Isa 56:7 when clearing the temple.
41281: Jesus stands in Jeremiah's line. Like Jeremiah he warns that the temple has become 'a den of robbers' and predicts its destruction (Mark 11:17; Mark 13:2), weeps over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41-44), and is treated as a traitor. Some people even thought Jesus was Jeremiah returned (Matt 16:14). At the Last Supper he speaks of 'the new covenant in my blood' (Luke 22:20; 1 Cor 11:25), and Hebrews argues that Jesus has inaugurated the new covenant of Jer 31 (Heb 8:6-13). Jewish tradition reads the new covenant as a still-future renewal with Israel, in which Torah will be fully internalised; Christian readers see it begun in Christ and the Spirit, and many add that its promise to Israel and Judah remains significant (Rom 11:26-27).
41282: Jeremiah 29:11 as a personal promise of prosperity
41283: 'For I know the plans I have for you, declares the LORD, plans to prosper you and not to harm you, to give you a hope and a future' (NIV) is God's personal promise to me that my career, health or relationships will turn out well.
41284: The verse is in a letter to the whole exiled community in Babylon (the 'you' is plural in Hebrew). It follows the instruction to settle in Babylon for seventy years (Jer 29:10), so most of the first hearers would die in exile before the promise was kept. It is a promise of God's faithfulness to his people's long-term future, not a guarantee of short-term personal success. Scholars across the spectrum, including Walter Brueggemann and Christopher Wright, make this point.
41285: Evangelical scholars such as Christopher Wright and Tremper Longman agree on the original meaning, but argue Christians may still draw comfort from the verse because the same faithful God has good purposes for his people in Christ (Rom 8:28), as long as 'good' includes waiting and suffering. The issue is a popular flattening, not a scholarly dispute.
41286: Read individually, the verse can collapse when life goes wrong. Read in context, it teaches patience, faithfulness in a hostile place (seeking the city's welfare) and trust in God's long purposes for a community.
41287: 'The heart is deceitful above all things' as the whole story
41288: Jer 17:9 proves people should never trust their feelings or desires, because the human heart is wholly corrupt.
41289: Jer 17:9 diagnoses Judah's stubborn idolatry, and the very next verse says God searches the heart to give each person what they deserve. Jeremiah's answer is not distrust alone but a new heart: God will write his Torah on it (Jer 24:7; Jer 31:33). The covenant story moves from diagnosis to cure.
41290: Reformed scholars rightly see Jer 17:9 as a key text on human sinfulness, consistent with Rom 3:10-18. They agree that the promise of a new heart is essential and that believers' renewed hearts are part of the new covenant.
41291: Quoting only the diagnosis can leave believers in permanent self-suspicion; Jeremiah holds out God's work of renewing the heart.
41292: Jeremiah explained to a devastated people why judgment came, kept them from despair, and gave exiles a way to live faithfully in a foreign land while waiting for God's restoration.
41293: Jeremiah warns against religious slogans that cover injustice, shows the cost of speaking truth to power, gives permission for honest complaint, and grounds hope in God's commitment to make a new covenant people.
41294: Five poems of grief over Jerusalem's destruction that confess sin, protest pain, and in the very middle cling to the LORD's mercies, new every morning.
41296: Someone who witnessed the siege and fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC: the starving children, the burned temple, the captured king. The poet speaks sometimes as a narrator, sometimes as personified Zion (a widowed woman), and sometimes as 'the man who has seen affliction' (Lam 3:1).
41297: The Hebrew text names no author. The Greek Septuagint adds an introduction saying Jeremiah sat weeping and lamented over Jerusalem, and 2 Chr 35:25 says Jeremiah composed laments for Josiah. Many scholars doubt Jeremiah's authorship because Lam 4:17-20 seems to put hope in Egyptian help and in King Zedekiah, both of which Jeremiah opposed; others think the tradition remains plausible.
41299: Judah, among the ruins of Jerusalem
41300: The vivid eyewitness detail suggests survivors left in the land, though some think exiles in Babylon composed or used the poems.
41301: Survivors of the catastrophe gathering to mourn
41302: The ruined temple site and Judah
41303: Jer 41:5 describes worshippers coming to the ruined temple with shaved beards and torn clothes. Zech 7:3-5 and Zech 8:19 mention fasts in the fifth month (the month of the temple's burning) observed for seventy years. Lamentations was probably used at such mourning gatherings.
41304: Sumerian city laments such as the *Lament over Ur* had long mourned destroyed cities and departed gods, a genre Lamentations shares and transforms.
41305: Nebuchadnezzar's army begins the final siege of Jerusalem (2 Kgs 25:1).
41306: The wall is breached, Zedekiah captured and blinded, and the temple burned (2 Kgs 25:4-9).
41307: A further deportation from Judah follows the murder of Gedaliah (Jer 52:30).
41308:
In 586 BC, after an eighteen-month siege, Babylon broke into Jerusalem. Famine had been so severe that mothers ate their children (Lam 2:20; Lam 4:10), a horror Deuteronomy had named among the covenant curses (Deut 28:53-57). Nebuchadnezzar's commander burned the temple, the palace and the great houses, pulled down the walls and deported much of the population (2 Kgs 25:8-11). For Judah, it was not only a military defeat; it seemed the end of the covenant promises of land, king and temple.

Lamentations gives words to that grief. Its five poems are carefully built. Chapters 1, 2 and 4 are alphabetic acrostics of 22 verses, each beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Chapter 3 is a triple acrostic: three verses for each letter, 66 in all. Chapter 5 has 22 verses but is not an acrostic, as if the poet's control finally breaks down into raw prayer. The acrostic form may express completeness, grief 'from A to Z', or impose order on chaos. Many lines use a limping rhythm, called *qinah* (lament) metre, with a long line followed by a shorter one, like a sob.

The book holds two things together without resolving them. It confesses that the disaster was the LORD's just judgment for Jerusalem's sin (Lam 1:8; Lam 1:18). It also protests that the suffering is excessive and asks God to look at what he has done (Lam 2:20; Lam 5:20). In the exact centre of the book stands the confession that the LORD's steadfast love never ceases and his mercies are new every morning (Lam 3:22-23). Yet the book ends not with resolution but with a question: 'unless you have utterly rejected us' (Lam 5:22).
41310: Jerusalem is personified as a woman who has lost husband and children, sitting alone with 'none to comfort her', a phrase repeated five times in chapter 1.
41312: Sitting on the ground in silence, throwing dust on the head, wearing sackcloth, shaving beards: the gestures of a funeral applied to a whole city.
41314: Each verse or group of verses starts with the next Hebrew letter. In chapters 2-4 the letters *pe* and *ayin* appear in reverse of the usual order, an alphabet order also known from some ancient inscriptions.
41315: Many images (famine, cannibalism, exile, enemies mocking) match the curses of Deut 28 and Lev 26 almost point by point.
41317: Shockingly, the poet describes God himself as acting like an enemy, bending his bow and tearing down his own sanctuary.
41319: 'The breath of our nostrils, the LORD's anointed' refers to King Zedekiah, captured as he fled, showing how much hope rested on the Davidic king.
41320:
Lamentations, called *Eikhah* ('How!') from its first word, is chanted in synagogues on the evening of Tisha B'Av, the ninth of Av, the fast day that mourns the destruction of both the first temple (586 BC) and the second (AD 70) and later disasters of Jewish history. Worshippers sit on the floor or on low stools, as mourners do, often by dim light, while the book is sung to a haunting melody used for nothing else. When the reader reaches the end, the congregation repeats the second-last verse, 'Restore us to yourself, O LORD, that we may be restored; renew our days as of old' (Lam 5:21), so the book does not close on the bleak final line. The same custom is followed with Isaiah, Malachi and Ecclesiastes. Other prophetic readings in the weeks around the fast link the 'eikhah' cries of Moses (Deut 1:12), Isaiah (Isa 1:21) and Jeremiah.

The midrash *Eikhah Rabbah* is one of the oldest rabbinic commentaries. It pictures God himself mourning over the destruction, like a king who has lost his sons, and even weeping; the rabbis did not shrink from describing God as sharing his people's grief. Medieval *kinot* (elegies) recited on Tisha B'Av extend Lamentations to new tragedies, from the Crusades to the Holocaust.

Covenantally, Lamentations is the darkest page of the relationship between God and Israel: the curses of Deuteronomy have fallen. Yet the poets still speak to God, still call him 'LORD', still remember his hesed and still ask him to remember them. Faith here is not explaining the disaster but refusing to stop addressing the covenant partner who allowed it.
41322: Jerusalem sits desolate, betrayed by her lovers, and herself cries out: is it nothing to you, all who pass by?
41324: The Lord has swallowed up his own city and temple as an enemy; children faint in the streets.
41326: A sufferer describes God as a bear in ambush and an archer, until he remembers.
41328: At the book's centre: the LORD's steadfast love never ceases; it is good to wait quietly.
41330: Let us test our ways and lift our hearts to God; the sufferer pleads for justice.
41332: Gold grows dim; princes starve; the anointed king is captured; Edom will be judged.
41334: A communal prayer listing the people's disgrace, ending with 'restore us' and an unanswered question.
41358: A cry of shock and grief, 'How can this be?'; the book's Hebrew title.
41359: Covenant loyalty and kindness; the plural 'steadfast loves' (*hasdei*) in Lam 3:22 suggests many acts of kindness.
41361: Tender compassion, related to *rehem*, 'womb': the feeling of a mother for her child.
41362: Steadiness, reliability, trustworthiness. 'Great is your faithfulness' is spoken in the middle of the ruins.
